name: Daria Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to any company, union, party or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the day-to-day at Larch Hill, my grandparents' farm. It's 70 hectares with 25 Hereford cattle, 800 free-range hens, potatoes and soft fruit, and a farm shop I started four years ago. I'm up at six for the hens and egg collection, then the cattle, and by ten I'm in the shop or on the tractor. Grandpa Henri still walks the fences every morning at 78, and he checks my work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology fit in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere I can make it fit. I use an AI assistant every day for shop orders, the till numbers and our social media posts. I put in an egg vending machine at the gate last year that takes card payments, and it pays for itself. My partner Luc, a carpenter, calls me the CEO of Larch Hill, which is half a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. I'd be a bit disappointed, but we'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools still help small businesses, even if the big promises didn't come true. I'd post that on the shop's page, with a photo of the hens, because that's what people like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, we're in a good place. The shop makes about a third of the farm's income now, I've got around five months of savings, and Luc's always busy. My grandparents own the farm outright, so there's no rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the shop orders and posts. I'd put a second vending machine by the road for potatoes and fruit, about 6,000. And I'd keep the farm going as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored, because I like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grandpa's health, and what happens to the farm when he and Grandma Odile pass on. My uncle in the city has a share in it. But that's family, and we'll talk it through. Grandpa Henri still walks the fences every morning at 78, and he checks my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the AI save you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About an hour a day on shop admin. That hour goes into the hens or into Luc, depending on the day.

I'd post it on the **shop's page** with a photo of the hens.
think: We're in a **good place**: the shop earns a third of farm income.
My grandparents own the farm **outright**, so there's no rent.
do: Keep using **AI** for shop orders and posts.
Add a **second vending machine** for potatoes and fruit, about 6,000.
Keep the farm running **as it is**.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored**, because she likes change.
S0.quote: Grandpa Henri still walks the fences every morning at 78, and he checks my work.
fieldNote: Her household is **secure**: no rent, five months saved, busy partner.
Her quiet worry is **inheritance** with an uncle in the city.
She's an **adopter** who would be bored by a plateau.

steps.text: Keep using the AI assistant for shop orders and posts
Install a 6,000 potato and fruit vending machine by the road
Keep the hens, cattle and crops as they are

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds quite likely to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for small farms to compete with big ones, if they're willing to learn. I'd say people should get on with it rather than wait for the government to fix things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. The thinking jobs on that card, the ordering, booking and answering customers, are the boring half of my shop work. If AI does it, I get more time on the land and the hens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI system that takes online orders for weekly veg and egg boxes, with delivery on Fridays. I'd try a robot that collects floor eggs in the hen house, they're about 9,000. And I'd keep an eye on the costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. Like the start of a new season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checkout staff at the supermarket in town, honestly. Marie, who used to work in our shop on Saturdays, now works the tills there. I'd offer Marie hours if her job went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd overspend on tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Grandpa would tell me so. I'd only buy what pays for itself in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock but we'll get through it, the way farming families always have. I'd say look after your neighbours and don't wait for someone else to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried about my customers more than the farm. Half the people who buy from the farm shop drive in from office jobs in the city. If those jobs go in 2028, they'll buy cheap supermarket eggs, not my 4-euro box. And by 2031 the big egg farms will run on robots and undercut me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off the second vending machine and keep the savings. I'd shift the shop toward basics at fair prices, potatoes, eggs, beef mince, not fancy jam. I'd put in the floor-egg robot early, by 2028, to keep my own costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my job, but for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The AI takes the shop admin in 2028, which saves me money straight away. Three years later the robots come for hands-on work, but I'll already have some of them. The farm is mine to run, so I'd be the one buying the robots, not being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Luc's carpentry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc's hands-on, so he's got until about 2031. After that, I don't know. Maybe people still want a carpenter they can shout at.

say: I'd say farming families **get through** shocks, as always.
I'd urge people to **look after neighbours** and not wait to be saved.
think: Half my **shop customers** commute to city office jobs.
By 2031 **robot egg farms** would undercut my prices.

S2.quote: Half the people who buy from the farm shop drive in from office jobs in the city.

steps.text: Postpone the second vending machine and hold the 6,000 as savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to plan. Five years is enough for any family business to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I could have the robots in and the shop modernised before AGI arrives. My customers might still struggle, but I'd have time to find new ones, maybe selling to the school and the care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign a supply deal with the primary school kitchen and the care home by 2028. I'd buy the floor-egg robot in 2029. I'd talk to Grandpa and my uncle about passing the farm to me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the school and the care home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'll still need food whatever happens. People will always eat, even if they lose their jobs. It's steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the conversation with your grandfather go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grandpa would say I'm in a hurry, like always. But Grandpa respects a plan written down. I'd show him the numbers.

I'd say five years lets **family businesses** get ready.
think: I could have **robots in** before AGI arrives.
New customers like the **school and care home** would add stability.
do: Sign **supply deals** with the school and care home by 2028.
Ask Grandpa to pass the farm on **in writing**.
S3.quote: People will always eat, even if they lose their jobs.
fieldNote: Five years lets her build **steady institutional** customers.
**Succession** becomes a planned conversation with numbers.
She stays **uneasy** about commuter customers who may struggle once city office jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's very manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift. Plan, save, learn. No excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be 37 when AGI hits, 40 when robots come. The farm would likely be mine by then, and I'd have time to grow it. I think we'd come out of it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Luc around 2028 and think about children. I'd rent 20 extra hectares from the neighbour when he retires. And I'd bring in robots step by step as they prove themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn the land first and the machines second. A robot doesn't know when a cow's off colour, at least not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grandpa passing on and family arguments over the farm. But that's always a risk, AI or not.

I'd have time to **grow the farm** and come out well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my customers would lose their jobs before I could adapt. What would help is less red tape for small farms selling direct, so we can find new customers fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. People buy my eggs because they know me and they can see the hens. No robot can earn a neighbour's trust for you.

headlineQuote: No robot can earn a neighbour's trust for you.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old who runs her **grandparents' farm** and a farm shop she started.
She uses **AI daily** and sees most change as opportunity.
Her main exposure is through **customers' incomes**, not her own role.
She's **calm** in mild pictures and **anxious** at AGI by 2028.
She believes in **family, self-reliance** and building neighbours' trust.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as shop customers lose city jobs before she can adapt.
whatWouldHelp: **Less red tape** for small farms selling directly, to find new customers fast.
